raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old female patient was admitted to our department with symptoms of fever, skin ulcers, subcutaneous nodules, and food regurgitation from the nose while eating. The patient is a farmer living in a rural area who was diagnosed with AIDS 2 years ago and started receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). However, she did not take the medications regularly and has been completely off them for several months. Four months ago, the patient experienced oral pain and found a purulent nodule on the upper palate. One month later, the nodule on the upper palate ruptured, forming a sinus that communicated with the nasal cavity, and the patient experienced nasal food regurgitation while eating. In addition, the patient had intermittent fever and multiple subcutaneous nodules on the trunk and limbs. The subcutaneous nodules gradually grew and ruptured, leading to non-healing ulcers. Throughout this process, the patient did not experience symptoms such as cough, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vision loss, visual field defect, or limb mobility disorders.
Upon admission, the physical examination revealed several ulcers and subcutaneous nodules on the trunk and limbs. The largest area of the ulcer was approximately 5*4cm2 and covered with necrotic tissue and purulent drainage. Subcutaneous nodules had mild tenderness and were poorly demarcated from surrounding tissues (Figure 1). The patient's oral mucosa had leukoplakia and a sinus tract with a diameter of approximately 1 cm in the upper palate that communicated with the nasal cavity (Figure 2A). There was also a small, unruptured, purulent nodule next to it. The patient's neck was soft, her vision was normal, and the superficial lymph nodes were not enlarged.
On admission, laboratory examination revealed a white blood cell count of 2.3 x 109/L, a hemoglobin level of 74 g/L, normal liver and kidney functions except for low albumin levels (28.7 g/L), a normal procalcitonin level, a C-reactive protein level of 21.7 mg/L, and a red blood cell sedimentation rate of 27 mm/h. The CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 4 cells/mul, and the HIV-RNA viral load was 94,000 copies/ml. Serological studies for (1, 3) beta-D-glucan, galactomannan (GM), and interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) were negative. Blood screening for syphilis, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus was also negative. Maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated thickening and enhancement of the sinus mucosa and partial tissue defects in the hard palate and nasal septum (Figures 2B,C). A chest CT scan revealed a mild infection in the left lung. Color Doppler ultrasonography of the right lower extremity nodule revealed a hypoechoic area measuring 4.0 x 2.8 x 1.7 cm located at 0.20 cm under the skin with an unclear outline, irregular shape, uneven echogenic areas, and small anechoic patches inside, which was considered an inflammatory mass.
The patient initially received treatment with fluconazole (200 mg daily), cefotaxime/sulbactam sodium (3.0 g q12h), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ) (0.96 g daily) to cover common bacterial and fungal infections. However, the patient's symptoms did not improve. On the second day of admission, the patient began experiencing recurrent high fevers with a temperature of over 39 C. The skin ulcers showed no signs of healing, and the subcutaneous nodules did not shrink. On the third day, a biopsy of the right hip subcutaneous mass was performed. Histopathological analysis, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) testing, and special staining of pathogenic microorganisms were carried out. Peripheral blood was collected for pathogenic microorganism mNGS at the same time. Additionally, cytological examinations of ulcer surface secretions and sinus secretions were performed. On the fifth day, the mNGS results of both tissue and peripheral blood revealed Acanthamoeba castellanii infection (The gene sequence has been deposited in GenBank under accession number PRJNA1108617). Pathological analysis of the biopsy tissue showed chronic suppurative inflammation with abscess formation, partial tissue degeneration and necrosis, and local granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cell reaction. Trophozoite-like structures were observed, which are considered to be indicative of an amoebic infection (Figure 3A). Tissue periodic acid-Schiff staining, Gram staining, silver staining, and acid-fast staining were all negative. Cytological examination of ulcer surface secretion also found amoebic trophozoite (Figure 3B). Blood cultures were reported as negative. Later, the patient underwent a head MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure measurement, and ophthalmological examinations. No visible abnormalities were found in the head MRI; CSF pressure and leukocyte count were normal; and glucose and protein levels were slightly elevated (glucose concentration of 4.85 mmol/L and protein concentration of 0.67 g/L). Cryptococcus neoformans capsule antigen, India ink stain, acid-fast stain, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus were all negative in the CSF. Bacterial and fungal cultures and cytological examination of the CSF were also negative. No retinal or corneal diseases were found during ophthalmological examination.
The patient presented with high fever, skin nodules, ulcers, and the formation of oral sinuses. Blood and tissue pathogen microorganism mNGS, histopathology, and cytology of ulcer exudate all detected Acanthamoeba castellanii, while other tests for bacteria, tuberculosis, fungi, and virus-related tests did not find any other pathogenic microorganisms. Based on the patient's clinical symptoms and test results, we considered the possibility of disseminated Acanthamoeba castellanii infection. Subsequently, we adjusted the treatment according to literature reports, choosing a combination therapy of voriconazole injection (0.2 g q12h), metronidazole injection (0.5 g q8h), and TMP/SMZ (1.44 g q8h). At the same time, local cleaning and disinfection of the ulcers were performed with the external application of ketoconazole cream. From the eighth day onward, the patient did not present fever again, the skin ulcers began to heal, and the subcutaneous nodules decreased in size. On hospital day 11, the patient restarted combined antiretroviral therapy (cART, lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/dolutegravir) and was discharged on the 15th day of hospitalization. On discharge, the patient was advised to continue itraconazole and compound sulfamethoxazole tablets for maintenance treatment. Three months after discharge, we conducted a telephone follow-up, but unfortunately, the patient had passed away. The family of the patient indicated that after leaving the hospital, the patient did not continue taking medication as advised and developed a new infection, which led to the worsening of the condition. The patient refused to be hospitalized for treatment again, which ultimately led to the patient's death.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old female farmer with AIDS presented with a 4-month history of a ruptured hard palate nodule causing nasal regurgitation of food, intermittent fever, and multiple ulcerating subcutaneous nodules on her trunk and extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to admission, the patient developed oral pain and a purulent nodule on the hard palate that ruptured 1 month later to form an oronasal fistula causing nasal food regurgitation during meals. Concurrently, she developed intermittent fevers and multiple subcutaneous nodules over her trunk and extremities that progressively enlarged, ruptured, and formed non-healing necrotic ulcers.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with AIDS 2 years prior and initiated on antiretroviral therapy, but had poor adherence and completely discontinued ART several months before presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent high fever (>39 °C after admission), oral pain, nasal regurgitation while eating, and multiple painful ulcerating skin nodules; negative for cough, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vision loss, visual field defects, or focal limb weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed multiple poorly demarcated, mildly tender subcutaneous nodules and necrotic, purulent ulcers across the trunk and extremities (largest ulcer measuring approximately 5 x 4 cm). Intraoral examination showed oral mucosal leukoplakia, an unruptured small purulent palatal nodule, and an adjacent 1 cm hard palate perforation/sinus tract communicating directly with the nasal cavity. Neck was supple, superficial lymph nodes were non-palpable, and visual acuity and ophthalmic exam (cornea and retina) were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukopenia (WBC 2.3 x 10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 74 g/L), hypoalbuminemia (28.7 g/L) with normal liver transaminases and renal function, normal procalcitonin, elevated CRP (21.7 mg/L), and elevated ESR (27 mm/h). Serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan, galactomannan, IGRA, syphilis serology, CMV, EBV, and routine blood cultures were all negative. Color Doppler ultrasound of a right lower extremity nodule showed an irregular 4.0 x 2.8 x 1.7 cm subcutaneous hypoechoic inflammatory mass at 0.20 cm depth.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 4 cells/µL. Maxillofacial CT demonstrated sinus mucosal thickening/enhancement and bony defects of the hard palate and nasal septum; chest CT showed mild left pulmonary infiltrates; brain MRI was normal. Lumbar puncture showed normal CSF opening pressure and leukocyte count, mildly elevated CSF glucose (4.85 mmol/L) and protein (0.67 g/L), and negative CSF cryptococcal antigen, India ink, AFB stain, HSV/CMV/EBV PCR, cytology, and bacterial/fungal cultures. Right hip subcutaneous nodule biopsy histopathology showed chronic suppurative and granulomatous inflammation with abscesses, necrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and amoebic trophozoite-like structures (negative PAS, Gram, silver, and AFB stains), and ulcer/sinus exudate cytology likewise identified amoebic trophozoites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated cutaneous and sinonasal/palatal Acanthamoeba castellanii infection (without CNS or ocular involvement) in a 63-year-old female with advanced untreated AIDS (CD4+ count 4 cells/µL, plasma HIV-RNA viral load 94,000 copies/mL). Definitive pathogen confirmation was achieved on hospital day 5 via metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of both right hip biopsy tissue and peripheral blood identifying Acanthamoeba castellanii (GenBank accession PRJNA1108617), corroborated by amoebic trophozoites on tissue histopathology and ulcer exudate cytology. After failing initial empiric fluconazole, cefotaxime/sulbactam, and low-dose TMP-SMX, targeted combination therapy was initiated with IV voriconazole (0.2 g q12h), IV metronidazole (0.5 g q8h), high-dose TMP-SMX (1.44 g q8h), and topical wound care with ketoconazole cream, achieving defervescence by day 8 and progressive ulcer healing. Combined ART (lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/dolutegravir) was restarted on day 11, and she was discharged on day 15 on oral itraconazole and TMP-SMX maintenance; however, she discontinued all medications after discharge, developed a secondary infection, refused readmission, and died within 3 months.
